tracks.title: The agent that can't let go
tracks.text: Lesson 08 point 8 — dispatch. A sub-lesson, under workflows. Here's the problem it solves. Ask a conversational agent — voice, or chat — for a twenty-minute research job… and you hit one of two walls. Either the turn freezes while it works, and you sit there listening to silence on a phone call. [sighs] Or it cheerfully promises to look into that… and then forgets, because the promise lived in a context window that ended. There's no hand-off seam. No ledger. No way for the work to reach back and say it's done. And if the agent does spawn background work… that work is usually invisible. Not in version control. Not reviewable. And when it dies… it dies silently. [curious] This lesson is the seam that fixes both halves. The parent — workflows, lesson eight — taught the grammar a plan is written in. This one teaches who calls the runner… how a goal becomes a plan without the agent writing it… and exactly how the answer finds its way back into the conversation.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: So — the definition. Dispatch is handing a goal across a seam, so the conversation never blocks. Four clauses, and we'll prove every one. First… a second model authors a workflow, per request. Second… a supervisor runs it, time-bounded, on a task ledger. Third… every terminal state queues as feedback. And fourth… the whole ledger renders to a file you can read in version control. The word is borrowed from a mail room, on purpose. You don't carry the parcel to its destination. You hand it to a system that takes it from there… gives you a tracking number… and lets you walk away. [curious] And every clause is proven by a single real run, that we'll follow the whole way down.

tracks.title: One goal, end to end
tracks.text: Now the keystone — one goal, end to end. Let me walk you through the whole life of a dispatched goal, as a story across five players. Picture five lanes. First, the conversational agent. Second, the router. Third, the author model — call it Mercury. Fourth, the task ledger. And fifth, the runner. The agent says one thing — dispatch, with a goal. The router turns to Mercury and asks it to turn that goal into an org outline. Mercury hands back a plan — a title line, then a set of TODO headlines. The router checks it has at least one real TODO. It saves the plan to a file under the workflows folder. It adds a task to the ledger — call it gee-kay two-oh-one — which flips from queued… to doing. The ledger spawns the runner in a fresh working directory. [excited] And here's the important beat — the router answers the agent immediately. Dispatched, true. Task, gee-kay two-oh-one. The conversation continues… in milliseconds. The single most important arrow is that one. The router answers before the runner has done any real work. Dispatch is fire-and-record… not fire-and-wait. The run executes on its own time… and the agent finds out how it went later.

tracks.title: The agent doesn't write the plan
tracks.text: Next — and this surprises people — the agent doesn't write the plan. This indirection is deliberate. The voice agent never authors a workflow. It hands a goal string… and nothing more. A separate, cheap author model turns that goal into a plan. That's the self-authoring demo — a goal in one model's voice… becoming a reviewable plan in another's. The author model has a default — Mercury — and it's called at a low temperature, because plan-writing wants to be boring and repeatable… not creative. It gets exactly one retry. If the output isn't a valid plan, the error is fed straight back — your previous outline was invalid, emit a corrected one — and it tries again. The validation gate is one line of intent. The output must contain at least one TODO-family headline with real text after it… or it's rejected. A plan with no tasks… is not a plan. Let me read you what Mercury actually wrote for our run. The title — research E2B and Daytona pricing. Then the first leaf — gather E2B pricing information — marked ordered, with a done-when check that a file exists and is non-empty. Then — extract pricing details from the E2B page, again ordered, again gated. And finally — consolidate findings into a report, writing everything into a single report file. Every leaf is ordered, so they run in sequence. Every leaf has a done-when gate that must pass before it can be marked done. And because the plan is a file before it's a process… you can read it, review it, and keep it. [curious] One thing to hold onto. Mercury wrote curl into that plan. The sandbox has no curl. The author is fallible — and that's exactly why writing the plan to a reviewable file is the right move. Hold that thought.

tracks.title: Four states, no fifth
tracks.text: Now the ledger — four states, no fifth. The ledger is a small in-memory process, holding tasks and their feedback. Every task is a record — an id, the goal, the plan file, a status, timestamps, a result. And the status moves through exactly four values. Picture the graph. A task is born queued. The instant the run is spawned, it becomes doing. And from doing, it can only reach two endings. If the run finishes, it becomes done. If it crashes, or runs out of time, it becomes blocked. There's no stuck… and no unknown. Those two blocked edges are the whole reason this is trustworthy. When the run launches, the ledger arms a kill switch — a timer set to thirty-five minutes. If that timer fires while the task is still doing… the process is killed, the status becomes blocked, and the result reads — timed out after thirty-five minutes. And if the worker dies without reporting… the task becomes blocked, with the crash reason captured. A crash or a timeout becomes blocked, with the reason… never a stuck doing. [excited] That invariant is the difference between a ledger you can trust… and a board full of zombies. And when a run does finish cleanly, the ledger keeps a verdict, not a transcript — a tally, like… four leaves done, two failed. That's all it stores.

tracks.title: Hearing back: the drain
tracks.text: So the run finishes, minutes after the agent moved on. How does the answer get back into a conversation that's already three turns ahead? [curious] Not with a callback that interrupts mid-sentence. With a queue… the agent drains on its own schedule. Let me tell it as a timeline. You and the agent are talking about something else. Meanwhile, the run finishes — and a note slips onto the feedback queue. The task id, the final status, a short summary. It just sits there. Then, on the agent's very next turn — about anything at all — the agent calls tasks. And that one call returns two things… the current task list, and a drain of the feedback queue, oldest first. And the drain clears the queue. So the agent turns to you and says — by the way, that research is done. That's the entire loop back into the conversation. No push. No ringing phone mid-thought. The feedback waits for a natural beat. [excited] The loop closes at conversation speed… not interrupt speed. The cost of that calm is one rule — read-once. The second time you call tasks, the feedback list is empty… because the first call already took it. Drain it, relay it… or it's gone.

tracks.title: A ledger you can read in git
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — a ledger you can read in version control. The ledger lives in memory… but it also renders itself to a file, on every single change. And it's a one-way street. The file is generated from the ledger… and never hand-edited. There's no two-way sync, because there's only one direction. Each field of a task maps to a piece of that file. The status becomes a keyword on the headline — queued shows as TODO, doing as DOING, done as DONE, blocked as BLOCKED. The goal becomes the headline text. The id, the file, the timestamps go into a properties drawer beneath it. And the result becomes a plain line below — the summary, or the failure reason. The verdict of all that, in one sentence — the rendered file carries every fact the ledger knows, in org's own grammar… so the whole task history is greppable, diffable, and reviewable in version control. It's the same move the board file makes — regenerated from the tracker, one direction, never hand-edited. Generated files… owned by the generator.

tracks.title: The orphan rewrite
tracks.text: And here's the best detail on the page — the orphan rewrite. The honest edge that makes the whole thing trustworthy. The ledger is in-memory. So when the engine restarts… every task that was doing is just gone from the process. But the last rendered file on disk still says DOING. The file would be lying about what's alive — claiming a run is in progress, when no process exists. The fix is a render correction… not a sync. On boot, before serving anything, the renderer rewrites the file in place. Any headline still in an active state — DOING or TODO — is rewritten to BLOCKED. And a comment is injected at the top to say why. Let me read you our real file, after the restart that orphaned our run. Line one — the title, groundskeeper, dispatched tasks. Line two — the injected comment — orphaned actives marked blocked on boot. And then the entry — blocked… research E2B and Daytona pricing — with its properties drawer carrying the id gee-kay two-oh-one, the plan file, and the start time. [curious] That's the full lifecycle in one screenshot, including the unglamorous ending. Gee-kay two-oh-one wasn't a failure. It was orphaned on restart… and the file says so plainly, rather than leaving a stale DOING to mislead the next reader. It's not pretending the work resumed. It's refusing to let a generated file lie.

tracks.title: What a run leaves behind
tracks.text: Another depth rung — what a run leaves behind. Underneath the ledger, the actual execution is the workflow runner from the parent lesson. And every dispatched run gets its own working directory, where it leaves a durable trail. Three things, specifically. First… a scratch folder — a persistent workspace the leaves read and write across the run. For our run, it holds the real extracted pricing — per-second numbers, down to fractions of a cent per processor-second. Second… a steps log — every tool call the leaf agent made, hash-chained and signed when the run is sealed, so the trail can't be quietly edited after the fact. And third… a telemetry database, written alongside. One rule governs the acceptance checks, and it's load-bearing. The done-when commands run in the in-sandbox shell… never on the host. An author-supplied check is untrusted input — so it must not become a way to run native code. [curious] And the consequence is that the checks fail closed. If a check names a command the sandbox doesn't know… the task simply doesn't reach done. A plan can't talk its way to success… by naming a command the sandbox refuses to run.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where it bites. The most vivid limit is the one I flagged earlier. Mercury wrote a plan full of curl and mkdir. The sandbox shell has neither. Let me read you two real lines from our run's steps log. The first — an error, unknown command, mkdir — on a pipeline that tried to make a folder and curl down a pricing page. The second — an error, unknown command, curl — on a pipeline trying to fetch the E2B page. The plan named the wrong toolchain. [curious] But watch what happened next. The leaf agent adapted. It reached for its fetch tool instead… pulled the pages… and still produced a pricing file with real per-second numbers. The run partially succeeded… despite the wrong instructions. And the gates that couldn't pass… simply left their leaves un-done. The plan is reviewable precisely because the author is fallible — and the gates fail closed instead of pretending. The rest of the bites are quieter, and all real. First… the ledger is in-memory. A restart orphans active tasks — and drops any feedback that wasn't drained yet. Undrained feedback dies with the engine. Second… feedback is read-once, and global. One queue, drained whole, no per-conversation routing. Third… summaries truncate to three hundred characters. The ledger keeps a verdict, not a transcript. And fourth… thirty-five minutes is a wall, not a suggestion. A run that needs longer is killed, and marked blocked. Dispatch is for errands… not marathons.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Why doesn't the agent author its own workflows? Deliberate indirection. The agent hands a goal — a separate model writes the plan. That keeps the talking model focused on talking, and makes the plan a file you can inspect before it runs. What happens at minute thirty-six? The kill switch. The thirty-five-minute timer fires, the process is killed, the status becomes blocked. No grace period — the bound is a wall by design. Can I hand-edit the tasks file? You can… but the next ledger change clobbers it. It's a generated view. Edit the work… not the rendering. Why org, instead of a job queue? Because the plan reuses the workflow grammar you already have — ordered leaves, gates — so a dispatched job is reviewable and diffable before it's a process. A queue row is none of those. Does feedback survive a restart? No. Both the ledger and its queue are in-memory. An honest gap, stated plainly. And — is this the same as the Autopoet? No. The Autopoet grows the system. Dispatch runs your errands, one bounded job at a time. Same supervision lesson… opposite subjects.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's dispatch. Hand a goal across a seam… get a tracking number in milliseconds… and hear back on your next natural turn. A plan you didn't write, run on a kill switch, recorded in a file that never lies about what's alive. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. The parent is workflows — lesson eight — for the grammar dispatch authors and runs. And just beside it, the agent — lesson five — for the leaf worker that does the job, bash-only, inside its sandbox. Everything dispatch does… is built from those two.
